lede: A vector written in components tells you how far across and how far up. Two questions are usually asked of it instead: how long is the arrow, and which way does it point. Both answers come out of the right-angled triangle the components make.
can: Find the magnitude of a vector with Pythagoras, and say what it means in context
Find the angle a vector makes with i, or with j, and check the pair adds to 90 degrees
Give a direction as a bearing when the axes are set to east and north

md: Components are convenient for arithmetic but say nothing directly about size or direction. Both are hiding in the triangle the two components make, and two results on the Unit 2 formula sheet pull them out.

md:
The $\mathbf{i}$ direction and the $\mathbf{j}$ direction are perpendicular, so an arrow with components 24 and 7 is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with those legs.

Pythagoras gives its length: $\sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25$. The magnitude is never the sum of the components, and never the larger one on its own.

explain: $36 + 64 = 100$ and $\sqrt{100} = 10$. Adding the components would give 14, which is longer than the arrow.

md:
The angle with $\mathbf{i}$ sits between the arrow and the x-axis. The side opposite it is the $\mathbf{j}$ component and the side beside it is the $\mathbf{i}$ component, so $\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}$.

Measure from $\mathbf{j}$ instead and the two sides swap roles, so the fraction turns over. The axes are at right angles, so the two angles always add to $90^{\circ}$.

title: Why the check works every time
md: The arrow, the x-axis and the y-axis meet at one point, and the axes are a quarter turn apart. The arrow splits that quarter turn into two pieces, so whatever one piece is, the other is what is left of the ninety degrees. That is why an upside-down fraction shows up instantly.

prompt: A vector makes an angle of 28 degrees with $\mathbf{i}$. What angle does it make with $\mathbf{j}$, in degrees?
explain: $90 - 28 = 62$. The two axes are a quarter turn apart and the arrow lies between them.

title: Magnitude and Direction
why: The same two calculations at a slower pace. Watch the triangle being sketched before the calculator comes out: that is the habit that keeps the fraction the right way up.

prompt: What angle, in degrees, does $3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$ make with the positive x-axis? Round to 2 decimal places.
explain: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{4}{3} = 53.13^{\circ}$. The 4 is opposite the angle and the 3 is beside it.

md:
If $\mathbf{i}$ is east and $\mathbf{j}$ is north, a bearing is measured clockwise from north, so it is the angle with $\mathbf{j}$, not the one the formula sheet prints.

The boat here has displacement $(40\mathbf{i} + 30\mathbf{j})$ m, so it is $50$ m from the harbour on a bearing of $053.13^{\circ}$. Read the stem for which direction the axes point before choosing the fraction.

prompt: With $\mathbf{i}$ due east and $\mathbf{j}$ due north, which calculation gives a bearing?
options: $\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
$\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
$90$ plus $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
answer: $\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
explain: A bearing starts at north, so north is the adjacent side and east is the opposite one.
